candidates.title: Novelty, diversity, and genetic dark matter in enterococci of invertebrates.
candidates.abstract: Enterococci appear to have originated in the guts of early terrestrializing arthropods and invertebrates over 425 million years ago-hosts that are now highly diverse and widespread in nature today. Yet most knowledge of the genus comes from human infection-associated lineages with genomes swollen by the recent accretion of foreign DNA conveyed by mobile elements. Because invertebrates dominate terrestrial animal diversity and biomass, they would be predicted to constitute a major but little-explored reservoir of enterococcal diversity. We therefore systematically examined Enterococcus association and species diversification in invertebrate hosts of the comparatively natural, isolated, but well-characterized environment of the Azorean island of Terceira. Over 100 invertebrate specimens were examined for associated enterococci, which were taxonomically classified by whole-genome sequencing. Supporting the existence of a large pool of uncharacterized enterococci and Enterococcus -adapted genes, 40% (eight of 20) of the Enterococcus species identified were either undescribed, including four candidate new species described here, or very recently discovered. In contrast, control isolates from vertebrates were exclusively of known species typical of sampling elsewhere, discounting geographic isolation as a main driver of the novelty observed. Further, because of the abundance of E. casseliflavus and E. flavescens in this collection, we obtained the resolution necessary to quantify the divergence and decipher the drivers of speciation in the controversial division between these naturally vancomycin-resistant species. These findings provide robust support for the existence of a large pool of new species and unexplored adaptive traits in invertebrate-associated enterococci-diverse environmental survival traits optimized for expression in an enterococcal background, and well positioned for transmission into human-associated enterococcal strains.IMPORTANCEEnterococci are auxotrophic gut-associated bacteria that co-evolved with their terrestrial hosts over many eons. In the last 75 years-the "antibiotic era" -E. faecalis and E. faecium gained genes for antibiotic resistance and enhanced virulence, emerging as leading causes of multidrug-resistant infection. Little is known about the source of those genes or the pathway by which they entered human-associated strains. A recent global survey suggested a potentially large repository of uncharacterized genetic diversity in the enterococci of invertebrates. We directly tested this prospect by examining enterococci of invertebrate hosts in a largely natural and pastoral environment. Our findings provide clear evidence that invertebrates naturally harbor vast unexplored enterococcal diversity. Moreover, associations are likely driven by intrinsic host selection factors rather than geographic isolation. This expands our knowledge of Enterococcus biodiversity, including the identification of four novel species, identifying a vast reservoir of enterococcal genes available to species that colonize and infect humans.

candidates.title: Protocol to stress human primary pancreatic islets with diabetogenic factors for subsequent single-cell RNA sequencing.
candidates.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease that destroys insulin-secreting pancreatic β cells. Using human islets is instrumental to understanding the initiation and progression of T1D. Here, we present a protocol for treating cadaveric primary human islets with inflammatory, immune, and viral stressors. We detail Coxsackievirus B3 expansion, primary islet cell culture, and treatment with diabetogenic stressors, followed by procedures for single-cell RNA sequencing analysis. For complete execution details, please refer to Maestas et al. 1 and Veronese-Paniagua et al. 2 .

candidates.title: Protocol for single-cell epigenetic profiling in human organoids and tumoroids with Epi-CyTOF.
candidates.abstract: In this protocol, we present Epi-CyTOF, a cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF) approach for single-cell epigenome profiling in cortical organoids as a model system for human brain development. We describe steps for in silico panel design, antibody conjugation and testing, sample preparation and staining, and high-dimensional data analysis. Additionally, we provide recommendations for applying Epi-CyTOF to other model systems based on our experience with gastroesophageal tumoroids. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Ditzer et al . 1 .

candidates.title: Cohesive modules of engraftment in fecal microbiota transplantation.
candidates.abstract: While single-strain probiotics fail to address community-level microbiota injuries in dysbiosis-related conditions and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) produces unpredictable communities, a middle-ground approach has emerged. This approach involves using small consortia of species, combining the precision of single-strain probiotics and the holistic approach intrinsic to FMT. The species selection in this oligomicrobial strategy is typically proprietary or based on studies linking single species to disease or health. To advance this approach, we developed the concept of cohesive modules of engraftment (CME) and a workflow for their identification from FMT trials. CMEs represent small donor microbiota subsets that engraft as units (modularity), while maintaining their original composition (cohesiveness). In benchmarking, we identified >200 highly cohesive CMEs (2-5 species) in 5 FMT trials and found evidence for cross feeding as a mechanism for CME integrity. Due to their predictable post-treatment compositions, CMEs deserve investigation as potential ingredients of future therapeutic microbial consortia.

candidates.title: Four decades of genomic stability and adaptive divergence in Xanthomonas phages: defining Duraznoxanthovirus arenicola and its evolutionary framework.
candidates.abstract: Bacteriophages (phages) are abundant and ecologically significant, yet their diversity and roles in plant-associated ecosystems remain poorly understood, limiting their application in sustainable disease management. To address this gap, we characterized 15 phages infecting Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni , the causal agent of bacterial spot on peach, has been isolated for over four decades from North Carolina orchards. Comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses revealed two temporally distinct clades with >95% nucleotide identity and 63 conserved core genes, forming a new genus and species, Duraznoxanthovirus arenicola . These findings challenge assumptions of pervasive genomic mosaicism, highlighting remarkable genomic stability alongside localized variability in accessory loci. Beyond genus-level characterization, our analyses support a broader taxonomic restructuring within the family Anamaviridae , introducing a new subfamily ( Terravirinae ) and two new genera ( Duraznoxanthovirus and Ralstopathovirus ). This work provides the a family-level framework for phages exclusively infecting plant-associated bacteria, offering evolutionary insights and a foundation for ecological studies and management strategies.

candidates.title: Seascape genomics uncovers contrasting population genetic structures in reef corals.
candidates.abstract: Abiotic conditions influence biodiversity and population connectivity, the assessment of which is critical for predicting climate change impacts and guiding conservation efforts. Coral reefs face severe losses, making effective conservation strategies increasingly urgent. Here, we use a seascape genomics approach to examine the population genetic structure of three non-model scleractinian corals around the Arabian Peninsula, a region with distinctive oceanographic features. We reveal contrasting patterns across species, which we integrate with geographic distances, larval dispersal models, and environmental data. Population structure appears shaped both by isolation by distance (IBD) and isolation by resistance (IBR), with environmental gradients often covarying with spatial separation. Our findings clarify coral diversification and evolutionary responses to conditions around the region. This work also provides a methodological framework to advance our understanding of processes structuring reef populations, thereby informing efforts to design robust marine protected area networks in the face of climate change and biodiversity loss.

candidates.title: Protocol for high-throughput identification of genes involved in pyroptotic cell death by live microscopy.
candidates.abstract: Intracellular lipopolysaccharide activates caspase-4/5 triggering pyroptotic cell death. We present a protocol for a high-throughput loss-of-function screening approach to identify interferon-gamma-stimulated genes regulating this pathway. We detail procedures for cell reverse-transfection with a custom-made small interfering RNA (siRNA) library in 384-well plates and priming with interferon-gamma. We then describe steps for transfection with lipopolysaccharide to induce pyroptosis and live-cell fluorescence microscopy using the IncuCyte S3 system to quantify cell death in real time without fixation. This approach enables reliable, high-throughput screening of cell death.

candidates.title: rchime: an R package for detecting chimeras in amplicon sequencing data.
candidates.abstract: A longstanding challenge in analyzing amplicon sequencing data is the presence of chimeras, which are PCR products that are formed by two or more templates. rchime is an R package that implements the UCHIME algorithm, which efficiently screens amplicon sequence collections for chimeras.

candidates.title: High-dimensionality approaches to the understanding and therapeutic manipulation of autoimmunity.
candidates.abstract: Autoimmune disease may arise from disruptions in immune architecture rather than isolated molecular defects. High-dimensional immunology now reveals dynamic cellular states, regulatory circuits, and tissue-specific immune niches, but translation into therapy remains limited. We propose an Architecture-Anomaly-Target-Lead framework that contextualises therapeutic targets within immune organisation and complements Reset-Rebuild strategies. Together, these concepts provide a framework for developing and evaluating more sustained, tolerance-focused treatment approaches for autoimmune disease.

candidates.title: Microbial Ecology at the Nexus of Food Safety and Biotechnology With Ecological Mechanisms, Risks, and Emerging Innovations.
candidates.abstract: Food systems are complex microbial ecosystems in which microorganisms play dual and often contrasting roles as agents of foodborne contamination and as essential drivers of food production and biotechnological innovation. Microbial ecology provides an integrative framework for understanding how microbial interactions, environmental conditions, and human interventions shape food safety outcomes and technological processes. This narrative integrative review is aimed at synthesizing current literature on microbial ecology at the nexus of food safety and food biotechnology and at identifying key research gaps and future directions. In this study, peer-reviewed journal articles addressing microbial interactions, contamination pathways, and ecological mechanisms relevant to food safety and biotechnology published between 2015 and 2025 were retrieved from major scientific databases and were synthesized using a narrative integrative approach. The review highlights ecological factors including microbial competition, stress adaptation, and biofilm formation across pre- and postharvest environments. At the same time, these same ecological principles are harnessed in food biotechnology to drive controlled fermentations, enhance shelf life through biopreservation, develop functional probiotics and enzymes, and engineer microbial systems via synthetic biology. Advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies, including whole genome sequencing, metagenomics, and multiomics integration, are identified as transformative tools for linking food-associated microbial community structure to functional outcomes. Despite significant progress, challenges remain in translating ecological insights into reliable industrial and regulatory practices due to microbial complexity, data integration limitations, and safety considerations. The review positions microbial ecology as a strategic framework for advancing food safety, biotechnological innovation, and sustainable food systems.

candidates.title: From bench to farm: leveraging Drosophila as a model insect for agricultural pest management.
candidates.abstract: The vinegar fly, Drosophila melanogaster, has contributed tremendously to advancing our understanding of the fundamentals of biology, from the chromosomal theory of inheritance to the survival of multi-cellular organisms in spaceflight. The use of this insect as a model organism has provided insights into all branches of life sciences, including agricultural and environmental sciences. In the context of integrated pest management (IPM), which often relies on species-specific natural history and phenology of pest insects and biological control, D. melanogaster flies have continued to be a powerhouse. In this review, we seek to summarize the use of the D. melanogaster model in studying insect biology relevant to IPM, with a focus on investigating the mechanisms underlying insecticide resistance. We sample case studies that adopt forward genetic approaches to reveal molecular underpinnings of IPM-relevant phenotypes and reverse genetic approaches that elucidate genotype-phenotype relationships. In particular, we highlight the contribution of D. melanogaster in understanding the biology and in developing IPM for the spotted-wing drosophila, also known as D. suzukii, a pest Drosophila species that devastates fruit production worldwide. Finally, we summarize recently developed research tools and resources in D. melanogaster that have potential utility for agricultural pest management.

candidates.title: Polaris: A toolkit for standardized construction, integration, and quantitative testing in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
candidates.abstract: Existing synthetic biology toolkits have expanded part libraries and assembly capabilities. However, new users may still encounter ambiguity in construct definitions, hierarchical transitions, genomic integration routes, and quantitative testing procedures. Here, we present Polaris, a Golden Gate toolkit for Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Polaris uses a MoClo-derived three-level hierarchy. Level 1 stores reusable parts, Level 2 generates transcription units and other intermediate constructs, and Level 3 supports multigene assembly and switching between testing and integration backbones. The toolkit distinguishes part interfaces from transcription unit interfaces, uses BpiI and BsaI in successive assembly stages, and provides parallel ccdB and mScarletI3 screening options. Integration modules and quantitative characterization frameworks were implemented in both hosts and demonstrated using representative genetic parts and activation and repression systems. A companion digital platform further encodes the Level 1 to Level 3 rules for assembly planning. Polaris connects hierarchical construction, stable genetic implementation, and quantitative testing within a common execution framework, providing a practical basis for data accumulation, part standardization, and future automation.

candidates.title: Plug-and-Play or Plug-and-Pray? Impact of random versus targeted integration on the linearity and orthogonality of synthetic gene circuits in CHO cells.
candidates.abstract: Predictable and tuneable gene expression is essential for advanced mammalian cell engineering yet remains challenged by genomic position effects and copy number variability. This study systematically compares random integration (RI) and targeted integration (TI) of two synthetic lineariser gene circuits, TetR/eGFP_Lin and PhlFd/mCherry_Lin, in CHO-S cells. Both circuits exhibited strong linearity and orthogonality across integration strategies, but integration method and repressor choice produced distinct performance trade-offs. RI increased achievable dynamic range for PhlFd but increased basal leakiness for TetR, whereas TI, via a dual-landing-pad system, constrained copy number, and reduced basal expression and PhlFd expression variability. These findings highlight integration context and circuit architecture as key design parameters informing rational design of synthetic regulators for biopharmaceutical applications.

candidates.title: Diverse oxidosqualene cyclases for triterpenoid biosynthesis.
candidates.abstract: Triterpenoids, a significant group of secondary metabolites, possess diverse skeletons and excellent pharmacological activities and are widely applied in cosmetics, medicine, and biopesticides. Traditional plant extraction and chemical synthesis cannot meet the needs of commercial production, and heterologous biosynthesis of triterpenoids has become a promising strategy. Oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs) are the key enzymes that determine triterpenoid biosynthesis. However, most OSCs exhibit low heterologous expression, low catalytic activity, and promiscuous catalytic products, which impedes the heterologous biosynthesis of triterpenoids. In this study, we constructed a dataset of 348 OSCs with known functions, which is the largest centralized resource of characterized OSCs to date. The 88 triterpenoid skeletons produced by these OSCs are classified based on their structural features, 49 of which have been experimentally characterized as the main products of OSCs, and the formation mechanisms of the common skeletons are summarized. Phylogenetic analysis and motif analysis elucidated the relationships among the sequences, structures, and products of plant-derived OSCs. Phylogenetic analysis showed that plant-derived OSCs were divided into two major clades, which corresponded to the biosynthetic mechanisms of the "protosteryl/dammarenyl" dichotomy. Motif analysis showed that 5 motifs are present in plant-derived OSCs, including 3 related to the catalytic activity of the OSCs and 2 related to product specificity. Finally, we summarized the common strategies for mining OSCs to provide directions for the discovery of novel OSCs and new triterpenoid skeletons. Our study will help discover or design OSCs with specific product profiles as functional elements for applications in synthetic biology.

candidates.title: Advances and perspectives in genetically encoded biosensors for biomarker detection and theranostic circuits.
candidates.abstract: Effective biomarker detection is critical for timely and accurate clinical disease diagnosis. However, conventional analytical methodologies are often constrained by laborious procedures, reliance on specialized equipment, and an inherent inability to perform continuous in situ monitoring. To circumvent these limitations, synthetic biology has pioneered the development of genetically encoded biosensors as a rapid, highly sensitive, and cost-effective alternative. This review specifically focuses on transcriptional regulation-based biosensors, primarily those utilizing allosteric transcription factors (aTFs) and two-component systems (TCSs). By integrating these regulatory sensing modules into engineered microbial chassis, researchers can achieve continuous, real-time biomarker monitoring even within complex and otherwise inaccessible physiological environments. This review particularly focuses on microbial chassis rather than mammalian systems due to their highly tractable genetics, rapid response kinetics, and their unique potential to be deployed as autonomous living probiotics for in situ theranostics. Furthermore, coupling these sensors with engineered actuator genes enables the construction of intelligent therapeutic genetic circuits. This closed-loop theranostic paradigm facilitates simultaneous, real-time diagnosis and autonomous, localized therapeutic interventions, paving the way for personalized and dose-adaptive precision medicine. Finally, we summarize recent advancements in these biosensor platforms, explore their applications in targeted disease interventions, and discuss the contemporary challenges alongside future perspectives for their clinical translation.

candidates.title: A 6His-2Flag dual-tag strategy enables high-yield production of antimicrobial peptide N6 in Pichia pastoris to combat multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumonia.
candidates.abstract: In response to the global threat posed by multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, this study established an efficient heterologous expression system for the antimicrobial peptide N6 in Pichia pastoris X-33. By employing an innovative 6His-2Flag dual-tag fusion strategy coupled with formic acid-mediated cleavage, we achieved a high-yield production of N6, with a final titer of 1.02 g/L-significantly surpassing previous reports and meeting the threshold for scalable industrial production. The expressed N6 exhibited potent and broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against clinical isolates of K. pneumoniae, with MIC values ranging from 2 to 8 μg/mL. Mechanistic studies revealed that N6 exerted rapid bactericidal and biofilm-eradicating effects through a multimodal action involving membrane disruption, metabolic interference, and induction of oxidative stress. In a murine systemic infection model, the N6 treatment significantly improved survival rates of mice to 70% and reduced bacterial burdens in key organs. This work not only identifies N6 as a promising therapeutic candidate against drug-resistant bacterial infections, but also provides a streamlined and cost-effective synthetic biology platform for the high-level production of antimicrobial peptides, thereby facilitating their clinical translation and industrial application.

candidates.title: Strategies and applications for alleviating carbon catabolite repression.
candidates.abstract: Carbon catabolite repression (CCR) is a widespread regulatory strategy across diverse microorganisms that prioritises the utilisation of preferred carbon sources. In industrial bioprocesses, however, CCR-mediated substrate hierarchy can delay the utilisation of secondary carbon sources in mixed feedstock, thereby extending fermentation time and limiting carbon conversion efficiency toward target products. Existing reviews have largely addressed CCR in a microorganism-specific manner, potentially obscuring conserved principles, limiting cross-species comparisons, and constraining generalisable engineering; computational modelling and engineering applications also remain underrepresented. This review therefore first summarises CCR mechanisms across diverse microorganisms through a common systems-level framework, in which transport-linked sensing converts carbon flux into intracellular signals, transcriptional regulators reprogramme genome-wide expression, RNA-based mechanisms fine-tune the timing and magnitude of responses, and protein stability shapes their persistence. Multi-omics approaches, particularly interactomics and single-cell omics, are then highlighted for revealing CCR as a dynamic and multilayered regulatory system by resolving interaction networks, temporal changes, and cell-to-cell heterogeneity beyond bulk measurements. Quantitative computational modelling is also discussed, with emphasis on kinetic and constraint-based frameworks that connect regulatory mechanisms to metabolic flux and predict system behaviour under changing carbon substrates. Engineering strategies, including adaptive laboratory evolution, transcription factor engineering, transporter and promoter engineering, and pathway rewiring, are further compared for the relief of CCR and improvement of substrate co-utilisation and production performance. Finally, these advances are presented within a Design-Build-Test-Learn framework, through which mechanistic discovery and omics-scale analysis are used to inform model development, and modelling and engineering are iteratively coupled to improve microbial performance. We propose that such an integrative paradigm is emerging as a unifying direction for CCR research, and provides a foundation for rational strain design and more efficient, sustainable biomanufacturing.

candidates.title: Reprogramming tumor vasculature: Integrating normalization biology with vascularized tumor-on-chip models.
candidates.abstract: Abnormal tumor vasculature is a hallmark of the tumor microenvironment that promotes hypoxia, therapeutic resistance, and disease progression while limiting the delivery of anticancer therapy. Although early anti-angiogenic therapies were designed to starve tumors by eliminating their blood supply, excessive vessel pruning often aggravated hypoxia and selected for more aggressive phenotypes. These observations led to the concept of vascular normalization, whereby judicious modulation of angiogenic signaling transiently restores vessel structure and function, improving perfusion, oxygenation, drug delivery, and anti-tumor immunity. In this review, we discuss the mechanisms governing tumor vessel formation, maturation, and dysfunction, and examine therapeutic strategies aimed at normalizing the tumor vasculature. We further highlight the major challenges limiting clinical translation, including the transient and heterogeneous nature of the normalization window, adaptive resistance mechanisms, and the lack of robust tools for longitudinal monitoring. We then integrate vascular normalization biology with vascularized tumor-on-chip platforms, examining how key features of the tumor microenvironment, including tissue architecture, extracellular matrix remodeling, hemodynamic forces, metabolic gradients, and multicellular interactions, can be recreated and quantitatively monitored. We critically evaluate how engineering design, biomaterial selection, vascularization strategies, perfusion, and integrated sensing influence the ability of these platforms to capture vascular normalization and therapeutic responses. By linking the hallmarks of vascular normalization to measurable on-chip phenotypes, vascularized tumor-on-chip systems provide controlled frameworks for investigating resistance mechanisms, optimizing treatment timing, and advancing precision oncology. However, challenges related to physiological fidelity, standardization, scalability, and clinical validation continue to limit their broader translation.

candidates.title: Enzymatic cross-linking collagen-based bioink for 3D bioprinting of endometrial model with endometrial epithelial organoids.
candidates.abstract: The human endometrium, a dynamic tissue responsive to sex hormones, plays a pivotal role in female reproduction and menstrual cycling, comprising diverse cell populations including epithelial and stromal cells. The development of in vitro endometrial models holds substantial potential for tissue repair, drug discovery, and disease modeling. However, the construction of biomimetic structural in vitro models capable of supporting long-term culture and preserving relevant biological functions has been hindered by limitations in both material properties and fabrication strategies. Here, an enzymatically cross-linked collagen-based bioink was developed, enabling extrusion bioprinting with favorable printability, biocompatibility, and bioactivity. The enzyme-catalyzed cross-linking process was optimized through room-temperature pre-crosslinking, and its evolution was described using a storage modulus (G')-time kinetic model, enabling prediction of the printable window and reliable fabrication of three-dimensional (3D) constructs. Then, monoculture and co-culture systems of endometrial epithelial organoids (EEOs) and endometrial stromal cells (ESCs) embedded in collagen-based hydrogels were established. Utilizing the bioink and printing strategy, an in vitro endometrial model was 3D bioprinted, exhibiting sustained viability (≥11 days) and hormone-responsive functions comparable to or showing enhanced functional characteristics relative to commonly used Matrigel-based or collagen-based systems. This biomimetic platform provides a physiologically relevant in vitro model for investigating endometrial biology, elucidating pathological mechanisms, and facilitating drug screening applications.

candidates.title: The application progress of detection technology for Bacillus cereus in food: Challenges, innovations and future prospects.
candidates.abstract: Food safety is a key issue of global public health. As a foodborne pathogen - Bacillus cereus (B. cereus), it is widely distributed in nature and can cause diseases in both humans and animals. The rapid detection of B. cereus is of great significance for the prevention and control of such diseases. This article provides a detailed overview of the development of B. cereus detection techniques in food, transitioning from traditional methods to a series of current technologies such as immunology, molecular biology and MALDI-TOF-MS. The principles, advantages and disadvantages of various detection techniques, as well as their application progress, were outlined. Furthermore, the application and advantages of combining different techniques in the detection of B. cereus in food were demonstrated. The CRISPR/Cas system possesses the characteristics of high specificity, high sensitivity and ease of operation, and shows great potential in the field of foodborne pathogen detection. This article also explains that the combination of CRISPR/Cas technology with RPA, LFA and AI technologies can further enhance the detection rate and accuracy. The aforementioned technology can enable the early detection and prevention of B. cereus in food, ensuring food safety and preventing the outbreak of foodborne diseases. This article has certain reference value in the research on the detection techniques of B. cereus and other foodborne pathogens in food, and provides strong support for safeguarding food safety and maintaining human health.

candidates.title: Studying the Effluent Quality of Enhanced Modified Ludzack Ettinger-oxic Settling Anaerobic Process (E-MLE-OSA) for Treating Real Municipal Wastewater
candidates.abstract: Background: Wastewater collection, treatment, discharge, additionally as reusing the treated wastewater in urban are critical factors for maintaining public health preventing contamination of water resources. This study aimed to investigate the performance of enhanced modified Ludzack Ettinger process-oxic settling anaerobic (MLE-OSA) process for treating real municipal wastewater in Sari wastewater Treatment, Sari City, Iran. Methods: To combine the OSA process technique with the MLE system, the Sludge Holding Tanks (SHT) were implemented in the return sludge line of designed pilot studies which comprised 1) MLE, which was regarded as the control system similar; 2) MLE-OSA4 with a 70-L SHT operated at 4-h Hydraulic Retention Time (HRT), and 3) MLEOSA6 with a 107-L SHT operated at 6-h HRT. To start the process, the overflow effluent of the primary settling tank of the Sari wastewater treatment plant was used. After 45-60 days, the reactors reached a steady state. The parameters of Dissolved Oxygen (DO), Oxidation-Reduction Potential (ORP), temperature, pH, Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD), Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD5), Total Suspended Solids (TSS), and nutrients were analyzed. Results: The results revealed that the average TSS, COD, BOD, phosphorus, nitrite, nitrate, and total nitrogen in MLEOSA4 effluent decreased 20.1, 14.6, 2.97, 10, 51.1, 19.3, and 20.7%, respectively compared to MLE. Similarly, in MLE-OSA6, the values decreased 34.2, 16.1, 14.6, 16.7, 69.6, 31.3, and 25.8%, respectively compared to the control process. Conclusion: Therefore, using natural wastewater, the enhanced MLE-OSA process showed better performance in removing the study parameters and better quality for the effluent. Furthermore, the quality of effluent is following the Iran Department of Environment (IDE).

candidates.title: Effect of Drought Stress, Soil Salinity, P. indica, and MWCNs on Biodegradation of Diesel Oil in the Pb- and Cd-Polluted Soil Under Cultivation of Triticale Plant
candidates.abstract: Background: Today, soil pollution with heavy metals and petroleum compounds is one of the main environmental problems. This research was done to investigate the effect of drought stress, soil salinity, Piriformospora indica (P. indica), and MWCNs on biodegradation of diesel oil in the soil that contaminated with Pb and Cd under cultivation of triticale plant. Methods: Treatments consisted of applying MWCNs (2% [W/W]) in the Pb- and Cd-polluted soil that was simultaneously polluted with diesel oil (0, 5, and 10% [W/W]), and the plants used in this study were inoculated with P. indica. After 70 days, plants were harvested, and plant and soil Cd were measured using AAS (atomic absorption spectrometry). In addition, the degradation percentage of diesel oil in soil was determined. Results: Soil application of MWCNs at the rate of 2% (W/W) significantly increased the biodegradation of diesel oil in the soil in the drought and salinity (6 dS/m) stress by 11.3% and 15.6%, respectively. In addition, plant inoculation with P. indica significantly increased the biodegradation of diesel oil in the soil by 12.3%. For salinity (6 dS/m) and drought stress, it was increased by 8.3% and 9.4%, respectively. In addition, the Pb and Cd concentrations decreased by 14.3% and 12.8%, respectively, when the MWCNs were added to the soil (2% [W/W]). Conclusion: Soil application of MWCNs and plant inoculation with P. indica not only increased the biodegradation of diesel oil but also decreased the plant Pb and Cd concentrations.

candidates.title: The Effects of Relaxing Music on Life Distress and Maternal-fetal Attachment in Pregnant Women
candidates.abstract: Background: Although pregnancy and motherhood are enjoyable experiences, they are associated with numerous biopsychological changes requiring adaptation. The present study aimed to assess the effects of relaxing music on life distress and Maternal-Fetal Attachment (MFA) in pregnant women. Methods: This was a quasi-experimental study with a pre-test, post-test and a control group design. The research population included all Iranian pregnant women referring to Laleh Hospital in Tehran City, Iran, in 2020. In total, 30 women were selected using the convenience sampling method and randomly assigned into the intervention and control groups (n=15/group). The required data were collected using the Life Distress Inventory (LDI) and the Maternal-Fetal Attachment Scale (MFAS). The intervention group listened to relaxing music for twelve 45-50-minute sessions in the morning and during routine midwifery visits; however, the controls received no intervention. The collected data were analyzed using Multivariate Analysis of Covariance (MANCOVA) in SPSS V. 22. Results: The obtained results indicated that the intervention group reported a lower level of life distress in the post-test, compared to the controls (P=0.0001, F=15.860). The intervention group also achieved a higher mean score on MFA, than the control group (P=0.0001, F=35.872). Conclusion: According to the present research findings, reproductive health, nursing professionals, and psychologists could recommend music as a complementary therapy to reduce stress and distress experienced by expecting mothers and to improve MFA.

candidates.title: The Role of Attachment Styles and Spiritual Intelligence in Predicting Women’s Emotional Divorce
candidates.abstract: Background: Emotional divorce refers to a situation in which the emotional relationship, support, passion, warmth, attention, love, and intimacy between couples (husband & wife) decline or diminish. Such conditions lead to an unaffectionate marital life to the point that the couples are only together under one roof. Accordingly, the present study aimed to explore the role of attachment styles and spiritual intelligence in predicting emotional divorce in women. Methods: This study employed a descriptive-correlational design. The research population included all women filing for divorce who were referred to marriage counseling and couple therapy centers in districts 5 and 6 in Tehran City, Iran, in 2020. In total, 400 women who met the inclusion criteria were selected as the study participants using voluntary response and convenience sampling techniques. The required data were collected by the Emotional Divorce Scale, the Adult Attachment Scale, and the Self-Report Measure of Spiritual Intelligence. The collected data were analyzed using the multiple regression analysis method in SPSS V. 22. candidates.title: Impact of Climate Change (CC) on Guava (Psidium guajava L.) Phenology, Yield and Commercial Fruit Quality; Prospective Policy
candidates.abstract: It has been observed that the climate is changing from last few couple of years. One of the many negative consequences of climate change is the alteration of the natural vegetation and environment. Phenology, or the shifting timing of plant growth activity, is one of the most well-documented consequences of climate change. Climate change is causing changes in the length of the vegetative and reproductive phases. By shortening the vegetative period, warmer temperatures often reduced the number of days needed for flowering in the majority of fruit crops. Guava (Psidium guajava L.) commercially 3rd fruit crop of significant economic importance in Pakistan and high nutritional potential, yet its production faces severe challenges during last two decades due to climate change overall globally and more frequently in South East Asian (SEA) countries. This comprehensive effort highlight and examines the climate change (CC) impact on Guava phen-phases, crop improvement and overall fruit quality parameters, highlighting disruptions caused by rising temperatures, altered precipitation patterns, and increased frequency of extreme weather events such as long summer season span, droughts and heavy rainfall during monsoon weather. These changes affect critical physiological processes, including flowering, fruit setting, fruit growth and maturation leading to irregular bearing, reduced yields, and compromised fruit quality such as, size, color and sweetness. Climate-induced biotic stressors exacerbate pest and disease pressures, further threatening commercial production. adaptation and mitigation precision horticulture strategies, including improved irrigation systems, canopy management techniques during high density plantation and efficient use of micronutrients like zinc and boron, are practical solutions to enhance resilience. the paper also explores future perspectives, emphasizing precision horticulture and supportive policy frameworks to ensure sustainable guava production. by integrating advanced technologies, resilient cultivars and innovative pomological practices, this study underscores potential to mitigate impact of climate change (CC) for secure guava production.
candidates.journal: Global Research Journal of Natural Science and Technology

candidates.title: Comparative Study of Efficacy and Safety of Ivabradine Versus Metoprolol in Stable Angina
candidates.abstract: Background: Stable angina pectoris, a manifestation of coronary artery disease (CAD), remains a major cause of morbidity worldwide, with India bearing a disproportionately high burden. Beta-blockers such as metoprolol are established first-line agents, but their use may be limited by adverse effects. Ivabradine, a selective If channel inhibitor, reduces heart rate without affecting contractility or blood pressure, offering a potential therapeutic alternative. Methods: This prospective, randomized, open-label clinical trial enrolled 100 patients aged 35–70 years with CCS class II–III stable angina and CAD. Participants were randomized to receive either ivabradine (5–7.5 mg twice daily) or metoprolol succinate (50–100 mg once daily) for six months, alongside standard background therapy. The primary endpoint was reduction in resting heart rate at four months. Secondary endpoints included frequency of angina attacks, nitroglycerin consumption, CCS classification, and incidence of adverse events. Results: Both groups were comparable at baseline. Ivabradine demonstrated a significantly greater reduction in angina attacks at 3 months (0.57 vs. 1.09 attacks/week, p

candidates.title: INFLUENCE OF ELICITORS OF VARIOUS NATURES ON THE ACTIVITY OF ENZYMES INVOLVED IN BIOSYNTHESIS OF LIGNANS IN CALLUS CULTURES LINUMA USTRIACUM L.
candidates.abstract: Summary The effect of mannan, β-1,3 glucan and ancymidol on the activity of enzymes involved in biosynthesis of lignans, podophyllotoxin, 5-metoxypodophyllotoxin and their derivatives production in the callus culture of Linum austriacum was investigated. The activities of L-Phenylalanine ammonia-lyase, Polyphenoloxidase, Tyrosinase, soluble Phenolase, wall-bound and soluble Oxidases were determined. Effects of elicitation on different steps of metabolic pathways in L. austriacum callus cultures were revealed. It was concluded that elicitors, which could stimulate the biosynthetic pathways affecting on activity of key enzymes, could stimulate the production of podophyllotoxins.

candidates.title: The co-existence of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency among individuals with hemoglobinopathies and their effects on red cellindices
candidates.abstract: Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and hemoglobinopathies are common among people of Duhok city in northern Iraq. The study was carried out to determine the prevalence of G6PD deficiency among individuals with thalassemia and sickle cell disorder, Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase was estimated in eighty-four (84) persons with hemoglobinopathies to observe its prevalence. A manual procedure was used to estimate the G6PD enzyme activity of fresh samples from the participants using BIOLABO SA, G6PD assay kit (Maizy, France).G6PD deficit was detected in 15(17.90%) of the case, (10.71%) of SCD, and (7.14%) of beta thalassemia syndromes with a statistically significant association between G6PD enzyme level and clinical diagnosis. No significant correlation between RBC count and RDW was seen between low and G6PD enzyme level individuals with hemoglobinopathies.The study emphasized the prevalence of G6PD deficit to be higher among individuals with hemoglobinopathy compared to the normal subject from a previous study from the same geographical region.
candidates.journal: Baghdad Journal of Biochemistry and Applied Biological Sciences

candidates.title: Data Science as a Catalyst for Audit Transformation
candidates.abstract: “In a world deluged by irrelevant information, clarity is power” Yuval Noah Harari, 2018 In the context of information society, digital transformation has led to an exponential growth in the production and storage of data, giving birth to what is known as data science, to address the need for new tools capable of smartly processing great volumes of data and transforming them into actionable information for decision-making in multiple environments. This scenario suggests that the old adagio by Hobbes (1651), “Information is Power” will soon be replaced by the newer “Clarity is Power” (Noah Harari, 2018) to more accurately convey the implications of a new model involving the management of data, information and knowledge. This is a unique opportunity for Superior Audit Institutions (SAIs) to exploit the potential offered by new technologies and the great amount of data generated within public agencies, and integrate them into their auditing processes to ensure a better management of public funds. Data science works as a catalyst for audit transformation, which strengthens SAIs’ independence while increasing public confidence and accountability. Data science methodologies can optimize audit processes, leading to audit reports of greater value, accuracy and scope, and more timely and relevant recommendations. High-quality reports foster a more effective and efficient public administration, having a significant impact in the improvement of citizens’ quality of life. Integrating data science into the auditing processes requires a roadmap that can guide SAIs in the use of these new tools.

candidates.title: Integration of Biomechanics and Digital Technology: Using Kinovea for Motion Analysis and Learning for Beginner Athletes
candidates.abstract: Background: The integration of biomechanics with digital motion-analysis technologies has introduced new approaches for examining movement efficiency, kinematic characteristics, and technical patterns in walking and running activities. Kinovea, as an accessible motion-analysis software, provides both visual and quantitative feedback. However, its application in supporting technique development among beginner athletes remains insufficiently explored. Aim: This study aims to describe the use of Kinovea in biomechanics training and examine its contribution to the awareness of kinematic characteristics and movement techniques among beginner athletes. Methods: A descriptive qualitative design involved 72 beginner athletes aged 18–25 years selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected over 16 weeks through interviews, field observations, and motion video recordings analyzed using Kinovea. Kinematic data focused on joint angles, stride behavior, and movement phases during walking, running, and the flight phase. Qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis with NVivo 12, while kinematic results were interpreted descriptively to identify performance patterns and areas for technical refinement. Result: Kinematic analysis showed coordinated joint-angle patterns across all phases. Walking analysis identified arm swing angles of 50.9°–58.8° and leg separation angles of 64.3°–67.2°, indicating a stable gait rhythm. The running analysis revealed knee angles of 68.8°–69.8° and elbow angles of 87.6°–89.1°, indicating efficient propulsive mechanics. The flight phase demonstrated knee angles of 81.2°–87.8° and elbow angles of 80.4°–88.3°, suggesting effective momentum use and postural stability. These measurements supported stride-efficiency assessment and technique evaluation. Qualitative findings revealed that Kinovea enabled athletes to interpret movement phases and identify technical inefficiencies through slow-motion and frame-by-frame visualization. Conclusion: Kinovea supports basic motion analysis by providing clear kinematic information and helping beginner athletes observe and refine their movement techniques. The findings also offer practical value for coaches by enabling more precise identification of inefficient patterns and guiding targeted corrections during early-stage training.
candidates.journal: Journal of Coaching and Sports Science

candidates.title: E2F4 gene therapy reverses established synaptic and cognitive deficits and remodels learning-associated signaling in Alzheimer's disease mice
candidates.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) causes progressive synaptic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline, yet strategies capable of reversing established deficits remain limited. Here, we show that neuronal expression of a p38MAPK phosphorylation-resistant human E2F4 variant (hE2F4DN), delivered by adeno-associated virus, restores hippocampal long-term potentiation and memory in homozygous 5xFAD mice after functional impairment is established. Treatment also reduces amyloid-{beta} and phospho-tau pathology and prevents hippocampal neuronal loss. Integrated proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses reveal remodeling of metabolic, redox, neuroimmune, synaptic-vesicle, and GSK3{beta}-associated signaling pathways. Following contextual fear conditioning, hE2F4DN-treated mice exhibit broader learning-associated synaptic proteomic signatures and distinct phosphoregulatory responses involving synaptic machinery. These findings demonstrate that E2F4 gene therapy can reverse established synaptic and cognitive deficits while preserving neuronal integrity and reshaping molecular responses to learning, identifying E2F4 phosphorylation as a potential therapeutic target for advanced AD states.

candidates.title: Magnetic nanoparticle enrichment reveals conserved nitric oxide burst responses in Arabidopsis and wheat
candidates.abstract: Rapid nitric oxide bursts are a conserved response to environmental stimuli, but their effects on cellular S-nitrosylation remain poorly understood. We developed a fluorinated magnetic nanoparticle method for rapid, efficient profiling of S-nitrosylation. Using Arabidopsis and wheat, we treated plant tissues with S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) to simulate a rapid nitric oxide surge. The method was then employed to capture S-nitrosylation dynamics within 24 h after treatment. Our analysis revealed sequence-dependent preferences for cysteines near basic or hydrophobic residues. Proteins showing rapid S-nitrosylation increases were predominantly associated with oxidative stress responses and energy metabolism, consistent with our metabolomic data. Functional studies using wheat TaGR1 mutants identified glutathione reductase 1 as a key regulated target. Modification at a conserved cysteine site rapidly modulated cellular glutathione levels in both species. Here, we provide an analytical tool and a multi-omics resource for investigating S-nitrosylation dynamics.

candidates.title: N-Hydroxypipecolic Acid Triggers Systemic Acquired Resistance Against Leaf Rust (Puccinia triticina) in Wheat
candidates.abstract: Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) represents a conserved immune strategy enabling plants to mount long-lasting, whole-plant protection following localized pathogen challenge. In Arabidopsis thaliana, SAR is orchestrated by the mobile immune regulator N-hydroxypipecolic acid (NHP); however, the extent to which NHP defines systemic immune states in polyploid crops remains unclear. Here, we establish NHP as an inducer of systemic immunity in hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum) during infection by the obligate biotrophic fungus Puccinia triticina. Local NHP application conferred robust disease suppression in distal leaves and elicited a temporally structured oxidative response characterized by a distal, biphasic reactive oxygen species (ROS) wave linking local and systemic tissues. RNA-sequencing analysis revealed that NHP induces coordinated transcriptional reprogramming, characterized by systemic activation of pattern-triggered and effector-triggered immunity pathways, WRKY-centered transcriptional networks, NPR1-associated signaling, and broad-spectrum resistance loci including Lr34. Concomitantly, targeted metabolomic profiling revealed a unique systemic accumulation of salicylic acid, salicylic acid glucoside, pipecolic acid, and NHP, without the conventional jasmonate signaling antagonism observed in eudicots. Despite this conserved immune architecture, functional analyses indicated divergence within the NHP biosynthetic pathway; while a single wheat FMO from sub-clade A2 was systemically up-regulated by NHP, the highly conserved TaSARD4 homeologs were constitutively expressed and functionally dispensable for rust resistance in planta. Notably, heterologous expression of TaSARD4-B successfully restored NHP-glucoside accumulation in an Arabidopsis sard4 mutant, confirming biochemical competence and suggesting alternative metabolic redundancies in wheat. These findings define a systems-level NHP-driven immune state in wheat and provide a conceptual framework for dissecting systemic immunity in cereals, extending SAR paradigms beyond model plant systems.

candidates.title: Is the Bitter Lesson coming to genomic prediction? An untuned tabular foundation model matches or beats specialized methods
candidates.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) is dominated by models designed around assumptions about how genetic variation affects phenotypes. Here we asked how well a general-purpose pretrained tabular foundation model called TabPFN-3.5 does with no genetics-specific modeling and no tuning when given marker genotypes directly. We benchmarked TabPFN-3.5 using a published comparison of 18 GP methods on 18 traits in six plant species. Against the published means, TabPFN-3.5 ranked first on 11 of 18 traits and had the best median rank. Because the published benchmark did not identify its test sets, we reran GBLUP, RKHS and elastic-net models on the same splits as TabPFN-3.5. Against the best of these, TabPFN-3.5 was significantly behind on only one trait, spruce wood density, and ahead on 12 of 18, with significant gains on all three soybean traits and rice flowering time. In the soybean panel, which had the largest number of lines, its advantage was clearest. In leave-families-out cross-validation, where models were trained on some soybean families and used to predict lines from other families withheld from training, every model lost accuracy and TabPFN-3.5 performed on par with GBLUP and RKHS. That a general-purpose learner matches or exceeds decades of specialized GP models is consistent with Sutton's Bitter Lesson, which holds that methods that scale with computation eventually overtake those built on human knowledge of the domain.

candidates.title: Endogenous Osteoblast-Osteocyte-Osteoclast Signaling Enables Bone Remodeling, Drug Response, and Cancer Invasion in a Nanoscale Calcified Bone-on-a-Chip
candidates.abstract: Bone homeostasis depends on spatially orchestrated interactions among osteoclasts, osteoblasts, and osteocytes within a unique microenvironment characterized by an extracellular matrix that is mineralized on the nanoscale. Reconstructing these interactions to enable autonomous cell differentiation and tissue remodeling remains a significant challenge in faithfully modeling bone physiology and disease in-vitro. Here, we present an engineered bone-on-a-chip platform that recapitulates the spatial organization of bone-resident cells, the differentiation of immune cells into osteoclasts, and calcified tissue resorption. We demonstrate that nanoscale mineralization of cell-laden collagen hydrogels is associated with ossification- and matrix-associated transcriptional changes and an osteocyte-like phenotype in osteoblast-lineage cells, while establishing a multicellular microenvironment associated with pro-osteoclastogenic RANKL/OPG signaling and supporting osteoclastogenesis and remodeling without the need for exogenous growth factors. Mineralized niche-driven osteoclastogenesis on-a-chip supported greater osteoclast differentiation than conventional stimulation with RANKL and M-CSF and reproduced differential responses to clinically used anti-resorptive drugs. The model further supports the integration of vascular networks and reproduces features of established tumor-bone interactions, including distinct spatial distributions of different cancer types within the mineralized microenvironment. Together, the findings establish a robust, self-regulated, and versatile microphysiologic model for investigating bone remodeling, cancer-bone crosstalk, and therapeutic interventions.

candidates.title: Engineering the Lr67-associated G144R substitution by prime editing enhances leaf rust resistance in wheat
candidates.abstract: Wheat rust diseases threaten global wheat production, highlighting the need for durable sources of resistance. The Lr67-associated G144R substitution in the sugar transport protein gene TaSTP13-D1 confers broad-spectrum resistance to multiple fungal pathogens. Here, we used an enhanced prime-editing system (ePPEplus) to introduce this resistance-associated substitution into the three TaSTP13 homoeologs in hexaploid wheat. Using the wheat-compatible JWPE1 vector, we achieved editing frequencies of 84 to 92% across the A, B, and D genomes in regenerated T0 plants. Homozygous edits were recovered in all three homoeologs, including one line carrying homozygous edits across all three genomes. Disease assays showed that edited lines had reduced leaf rust severity and fungal biomass compared with susceptible controls. Notably, the line carrying edits in all three homoeologs exhibited the greatest reduction in fungal biomass. These results demonstrate the potential of prime editing to directly introduce resistance-associated alleles into wheat and provide a strategy for accelerating the development of rust-resistant cultivars.

candidates.title: Primate Saccade Rhythmicity
candidates.abstract: Rhythmic sampling is a hallmark of many sensory systems across diverse organisms. In primate vision, rapid foveating eye movements repetitively sample the visual environment at a rate of approximately 4 Hz. Yet, the observed inter-saccadic interval distributions might equally well be produced by a non-rhythmic stochastic process as by a - putatively variable- rhythmic generator. This raises the fundamental question whether primate visual sampling differs from the numerous examples of rhythmic sampling strategies exhibited across sensory modalities and species. Here, using experiments in humans, macaques, and a marmoset, as well as statistical approaches adopted from studies of temporal structure in neuronal spiking patterns, we show that primate saccade generation is unambiguously rooted in a rhythmic source. This finding was remarkably consistent across the three primate species despite their significant evolutionary distance. Importantly, we find that saccade rate undergoes smooth, slow fluctuations on the scale of seconds, and accounting for those rate fluctuations was crucial for revealing the true degree of saccade rhythmicity. Thus, exact saccade timing is determined by an interaction between the slow saccade-rate fluctuations and the more temporally-local rhythmic generator. This demonstration of rhythmicity in overt oculomotor sampling behavior provides a link to the fundamentally rhythmic nature of many central perceptual and cognitive processes, and places primate saccadic sampling into the large family of rhythmic active sampling behaviors.

candidates.title: EPHB2 promotes long-range axon extension and its variants cause callosal dysgenesis
candidates.abstract: The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest fibre tract connecting the cerebral hemispheres, essential for integrating neural activity across large-scale brain networks. Accordingly, abnormal CC development is associated with diverse neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Callosal projection neurons (CPNs) of the cortex form the CC by extending long-range axons to the contralateral hemisphere; however, the mechanisms that sustain axon elongation over such remarkable distances remain poorly understood. Here we show that variants in the human gene EPHB2, which encodes a tyrosine kinase receptor regulating nervous system development and implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, cause CC dysgenesis. We characterise variant- specific effects on EPHB2 signalling and demonstrate that variants identified in individuals with distinct CC morphologies differentially alter CPN axon outgrowth and integration in vivo. We further show that EphB2 has a cell-autonomous, ligand-independent function in promoting CPN axon outgrowth by spatially organising actomyosin at axonal growth cones. These findings reveal a previously unrecognised role for EphB2 in promoting long-range axon extension and provide the first evidence that EPHB2 variants cause CC dysgenesis in humans. More broadly, our study links molecular variation in EPHB2 to individualised abnormalities in brain connectivity and provides a framework for understanding how heterogeneous circuit-level phenotypes arise in neurodevelopmental disorders.

candidates.title: Mathematical model for visual cortical development based on molecular mechanisms underlying the generation and elimination of dendritic spines
candidates.abstract: In the developing brain, neural circuits are elaborated by the activity-dependent rewiring of synaptic connections. The current view of synaptic rewiring in early development is that filopodia spontaneously generated along dendrites transform into spines by establishing contacts with neighboring axonal boutons to form synapses whereas spines of inappropriate synapses are eliminated in an activity-dependent manner. In this theoretical study, we mainly focus on the processes of spine generation, maturation, and elimination to build a mathematical model of synaptic rewiring, incorporating experimental findings on actin polymerization and depolymerization under the activation of Rho-GTPases mediated by the binding of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) to neurotrophin receptors such as tropomyosin kinase receptor B (TrkB) and the low-affinity-nerve growth factor receptor (p75NTR). TrkB receptors are dephosphorylated by chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans (CSPGs) mediated by protein-tyrosine phosphatase {sigma} (PTP{sigma} in an age-dependent manner. The model describes the generation or elimination of dendritic spines of visual cortical neurons under actin polymerization and depolymerization to establish appropriate synaptic contacts on afferent fibers of cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus. The simulations based on the model reproduced not only simple-cell-like receptive fields and orientation-direction maps but also a characteristic profile of the total number of synapses, which shows an early increase and a delayed decrease during the critical period. It is also demonstrated that the formation of direction selectivity is delayed behind the formation of orientation selectivity, which is likely promoted by the pruning of inappropriate synapses.

candidates.title: A new therapeutic opportunity in Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever: Targeting the stalk domain of viral nucleocapsid protein for therapeutic intervention
candidates.abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a high-consequence pathogen for which no approved antivirals or vaccines exist. The viral nucleocapsid protein (N protein) is central to the Nairovirus life cycle, coordinating genomic RNA encapsidation and selective enhancement of viral mRNA translation through its interaction with the panhandle-like hairpin structure in the S-segment mRNA 5′ untranslated region (UTR). Here, we developed a robust fluorescence polarization anisotropy (FPA) based high-throughput assay capable of quantitatively monitoring the interaction between purified N protein and the viral 5′UTR hairpin. The assay demonstrated excellent stability, DMSO tolerance, and performance metrics (average Z′ > 0.6), enabling the screening of 108,947 small molecules. Primary screening identified 122 inhibitors, 86 of which showed clear dose-responsive activity. Cluster analysis, medicinal chemistry filtering, and repurchase-based validation yielded 37 confirmed hits, from which compounds 11, 14, and 33 were prioritized for further testing. Biochemical analysis demonstrated that all three compounds noncompetitively inhibit N protein–UTR binding with IC₅₀ values of 11–41 μM. These compounds exhibited minimal cytotoxicity (CC₅₀ > 1–2 mM) and potent antiviral activity in cell culture against Hazara virus (HZV), a BSL-2 surrogate for CCHFV, with EC₅₀ values of ~23–51 μM and favorable selectivity indices (>34–86). Plaque assays further showed that compounds 11 and 14 reduced the production of infectious viral particles by over 100-fold, whereas compound 33 nearly eliminated detectable infectious virus in the media. Mechanistic assays revealed that these inhibitors act during post-entry steps and selectively block the N protein–mediated enhancement of viral mRNA translation without affecting the canonical host translation machinery. Molecular modeling and biochemical/translation assays support binding of compound 11 to the N protein stalk–head interface, involving residues Gln300, Glu240 and Lys473. Collectively, these findings identify the N protein–5′UTR interface as a tractable antiviral target and establish first-in-class small-molecule inhibitors that disrupt essential Nairovirus RNA–N protein interaction. These compounds provide strong leads for further optimization and development of urgently needed therapeutics for CCHFV. Author summary: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a dangerous tick-borne virus illness has no approved treatments at present. The virus relies on a key nucleocapsid protein to efficiently translate its mRNA once it enters human cells. The main focus of this study was to find small molecule inhibitors for this protein that could essentially shut down the virus replication inside the cells. To do this, we developed a new high-throughput screening approach that allowed us to rapidly evaluate more than 100,000 chemical compounds. From this large search, we found three promising molecules that disrupt a crucial interaction between the viral nucleocapsid protein and a unique hairpin structure on the viral mRNA. What makes these compounds exciting is that they inhibit the virus replication after it has already entered cells, without being toxic to the host cells. These findings highlight an entirely new antiviral strategy: targeting the way a virus hijacks the host’s translation machinery for the preferential translation of its own mRNA. By blocking this early step in viral gene expression, we can potentially stop infection before it takes hold. This work not only advances antiviral drug discovery, but also deepens our understanding of how viruses manipulate host pathways during infection.

candidates.title: Immune evasion in Mucorales species: From stealth spores to angioinvasive hyphae
candidates.abstract: Mucormycosis is an invasive fungal infection caused by members of the order Mucorales, which employ stage- and species-specific mechanisms to evade host immunity. Resting spores of experimentally studied Rhizopus species can persist after macrophage uptake because macrophages restrict germination but do not efficiently kill all internalized resting spores. Germination is accompanied by cell-wall remodeling and increased β-glucan exposure in several experimentally examined Mucorales species; however, functional Dectin-1-dependent responses have been demonstrated most clearly in Rhizopus and its conservation across species and isolates remains incompletely defined. Studies predominantly in Rhizopus delemar identify fungal CotH proteins as ligands for host GRP78 or integrin α3β1, linking invasion to tissue-specific host pathways. Intracellular survival also varies across species: Rhizopus spores remain dormant and prevent phagosome maturation, whereas Mucor circinelloides can germinate within macrophages via stress-response and calcineurin-dependent mechanisms. Cunninghamella shows a significant resistance to neutrophil damage, while other Mucorales species suppress accumulation of nitric oxide in activated macrophages. Studies of Rhizopus reveal morphology-dependent dendritic-cell activation and Th17 polarization, and that Rhizopus-specific T cells can directly damage fungal hyphae. Whether such adaptive responses are present in other Mucorales species remains unknown. Understanding these immune evasion mechanisms could support the development of therapies focused on cytokines, adoptive T-cells, and CotH-targets.

candidates.title: GEI-17-mediated SUMOylation of GDP dissociation inhibitor GDI-1 regulates apoptotic cell clearance
candidates.abstract: by Lei Yuan, Peiyao Li, Aiying Ma, Chao Li, Fuqiao Liu, Yunmin Xie, Qian Zheng, Hui Wang, Hui Xiao Apoptotic cell clearance represents the final stage of apoptosis and involves phagosome formation, maturation, and digestion. Here, we found that SUMO modifications participate in apoptotic cell clearance by influencing phagosomal degradation activity in C. elegans . The SUMO E3 ligase, GEI-17, SUMOylates GDP dissociation inhibitor (GDI-1) at K270 to trigger phagosomal degradation. Upon SUMOylation, GDI-1 facilitates release of GDP-bound RAB-1, which is subsequently converted to the GTP-bound form in a manner dependent on GDI displacement factor, PRAF-3. RAB-1 conversion enables binding and translocation of RAB-7 from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to promote phagosome maturation and degradation activity. In the absence of GDI-1 SUMOylation, GDI-1 binds to GDP-RAB-1, sequestering it in the cytoplasm, resulting in impaired phagosomal degradation. Furthermore, we found SUMOylation of GDI1 at a conserved site plays a crucial role in efferocytosis regulation in mammals. This study defines a previously unrecognized mechanism by which SUMOylation drives apoptotic cell clearance.

candidates.title: Local feedback governs cell fate transition to drive self-organized phenotypic equilibrium in hierarchical tumors
candidates.abstract: by Emma Legait, Charlotte Rulquin, Lauranne Bouteille, Raphaël Clément, Cédric Maurange How cell-state transitions are regulated along a tumor lineage to determine its overall cellular composition remains unclear. Using a simple hierarchical tumor model in Drosophila , we show that differentiation of cancer stem cells (CSCs) into transit amplifying progenitors (TAPs) depends on the fraction of TAPs among their immediate neighbors. This relationship is captured by a local feedback transition rule that quantitatively predicts CSC transition probability. Implementing this rule in 3D growth simulations spontaneously recapitulates CSC clustering and the emergence of a stable CSC fraction within tumors. Mechanistically, the local feedback is mediated by EGFR signaling from newly produced TAPs, propagating differentiation across CSC clusters. Consistently, we show that clustering protects the CSC pool from depletion driven by surrounding TAPs, indicating that spatial architecture and lineage dynamics are tightly coupled. Together, these findings show that a local feedback governing fate transitions drives emergent spatial organization that stabilizes the stem cell fraction in hierarchical tumors.

candidates.title: Migration as a key influence on ungulate eco-evolutionary history
candidates.abstract: by Gustavo Burin Species can overcome resource limitations by migrating to more favourable areas. A new study in PLOS Biology shows that migration has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, that likely led to changes in ecosystem functioning. Species can overcome environmental limitations by migrating to more favorable areas. This Primer explores a new study in PLOS Biology showing that this behavior has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, which in turn likely led to changes in ecosystem properties and functioning.

candidates.title: An indirect wing steering muscle stabilizes flight by regulating wing pitch angle in Drosophila
candidates.abstract: by Han Kheng Teoh, Debojyoti Biswas, Haoru Li, Abby Leung, B. Kemper Ludlow, Samuel C. Whitehead, Erica Ehrhardt, Michael Dickinson, Tsevi Beatus, Noah J. Cowan, Itai Cohen Flapping flight is inherently unstable, requiring Drosophila to fine-tune their wing motions on a milliseconds timescale. Pioneering studies have shown that the direct steering muscles, which attach to the wing hinge, are important for generating these rapid flight reflexes. Recent connectome data, however, reveal that indirect steering muscles or tension muscles, which alter the mechanics of the thorax, receive some of the same synaptic inputs from the sensory apparatus as the direct steering muscles. This discovery suggests that the indirect steering muscles may also be important for flight control. Here, we show that the indirect tergopleural muscles indeed contribute substantially to stabilization, particularly for large pitch perturbations. We find that for small perturbations (less than 1,000 °/s), flies modulate their wing stroke amplitude to generate lift-based corrective torques, a strategy that has been previously documented. For larger perturbations, however, we observe that Drosophila engage an additional wing degree of freedom—the wing pitch angle—to leverage additional lift and drag forces during the corrective maneuver. Quasi-steady aerodynamic simulations reveal that this strategy minimizes power consumption, anaolgous to how some mammals (including humans) adjust their steady-state gaits in a near energy-optimal manner. Using optogenetics and a control theory framework, we demonstrate that the tergopleural muscle is activated by a proportional gain component of a nonlinear proportional-integral controller responsible for determining the wing pitch angle during large perturbations. A simplified torsional spring model for the wing hinge captures the changes in the wing pitch dynamics observed during correction maneuvers by using the tergopleural muscle to adjust the rest angle of the wing. These findings provide a striking example of reflex strategy selection in time-critical behaviors and underscore the vital role of indirect steering muscles in flight stabilization.

candidates.title: Dynamic functional connectivity reveals evolving neural activity states of alcohol-seeking in rats
candidates.abstract: by Yujing Zhang, Nicholas M. Timme, Mintao Liu, Christopher C. Lapish, Joaquín Goñi The brain mechanisms underlying persistent alcohol-seeking in Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) remain incompletely understood. To investigate this behavior, we characterized the temporal evolution of neural activity states in the anterior cingulate cortex of freely behaving rats performing an aversion-resistant drinking (ARD) task. Alcohol-preferring (P) rats were assessed, as they reliably exhibit ARD when alcohol is devalued with the bitter tastant quinine. P rats were compared with Wistar rats, which progress slower to ARD, as indicated by cessation of drinking following quinine devaluation. Using dynamic functional connectivity analyses of spike-train recordings, we identified latent neural states corresponding to seeking and non-seeking phases. We then integrated the latent-state decoding of neural activity with a seeking intensity model derived from the observed drinking behavior. This framework revealed that the decoded latent neural states closely tracked behavior. Furthermore, during alcohol-reinforced sessions, neural and behavioral measures of drinking or non-drinking states were strongly aligned in both strains. However, after alcohol devaluation, this alignment diverged in P rats but remained consistent in Wistars. The inability of P rats to acquire stable neural states following devaluation suggests impaired formation of latent states as a neural mechanism of ARD, offering insights into the cognitive vulnerabilities that may sustain AUD.

candidates.title: Allosteric inhibition rescues hydrocephalus caused by catalytically inactive Shp2 in mice
candidates.abstract: by Neoklis Makrides, Emily Sun, Hilal Mir, Jen-Zen Chuang, Ziyuan Jiang, Yihua Wu, Carlos Serra, John Peregrin, Qian Wang, Wellington V. Cardoso, Ching-Hwa Sung, Neel H. Shah, Xin Zhang SHP2, a protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) crucial in Ras-MAPK signaling, is associated with various human congenital diseases and cancers. Here, we show that the catalytically inactive Shp2 C459S mutation results in communicating hydrocephalus, similar to the catalytically activating Shp2 E76K and Mek1 DD mutants. Unlike previous mutants, however, Shp2 C459S/+ mutation uniquely affects ciliary development rather than neurogenesis, leading to structural abnormalities in cilia and impaired ciliary motility. Differential scanning fluorimetry suggested that SHP2 C459S , SHP2 E76K , and SHP2 C459S/E76K mutations all induce an open SHP2 conformation, but only SHP2 C459S leads to aberrant GAB1 phosphorylation in cells expressing wild-type SHP2. Consistent with this distinct signaling profile, brain ventricular tissues from Shp2 C459S/+ mice exhibit elevated GAB1 and AKT phosphorylation despite normal ERK and STAT3 activities, implicating dysregulated PI3K–AKT signaling in the pathogenesis of hydrocephalus. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of PI3K markedly rescues ciliogenesis defects and alleviates hydrocephalus in mutant mice. Furthermore, the allosteric SHP2 inhibitor SHP099 increases the thermal stability of SHP2C459S protein, consistent with a shift toward a closed state, and ameliorates hydrocephalus in Shp2 C459S/+ mice. These findings suggest that, in this engineered mouse model, Shp2 -associated hydrocephalus is driven by conformational changes rather than altered catalytic activity. Our results underscore the therapeutic potential of conformation-specific allosteric inhibitors in targeting both catalytically active and inactive SHP2 mutants.
